<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:degree}
The $k$-th derivative of a degree-$k$ spline is piecewise constant and its $(k{+}1)$-th derivative
vanishes almost everywhere. A residual of order $p$ therefore needs $k\ge p+1$ for the $p$-th
derivative to be continuous. We set $k=\max(3,p+1)$, i.e.\ $k=3,3,3,4,5$ for P1 to P5.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:scale}
On a grid of spacing $h$ the $p$-th derivative of a B-spline scales like $h^{-p}$. For $p=3,4$ a
fine grid therefore produces residual gradients that are several orders of magnitude larger than those of
a coarse grid, and the optimization stalls. In a pilot study (training loss only, \cref{sec:pilot})
$G=10$ left the Falkner-Skan loss on the trivial plateau, while $G=5$ and $G=3$ converged, and on the fourth-order problem $G=3$ was clearly better than $G=5$. We therefore train on a
coarse grid and add resolution by grid extension (\cref{sec:gridext}).
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:nested}
Grid extension \citep{liu2024kan} replaces the grid of a trained B-spline KAN by a finer one and fits the new
coefficients to the old spline by least squares. If the new knots are placed independently of the old ones,
the fit preserves the values of $\phi_{ij}$ only approximately and its $p$-th derivative much less so, and
a $p$-th order residual jumps after the extension. If instead every old knot is kept
and each interval is subdivided (knot insertion \citep{boehm1980,cohen1980}), the old spline space is a subspace of the new one, so the
old spline is represented \emph{exactly}, with all its derivatives, and the physics loss is unchanged by
the extension. We use this nested refinement, doubling the number of intervals on the knot span covered by
the data at each extension.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
